title: Strategy Is the Art of Sacrifice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post redefines strategy as the discipline of choosing what not to do. Because time, money, talent and attention are finite, leaders who chase every opportunity dilute their advantage. The author argues that every Yes carries a hidden No, illustrating with quality versus low cost, speed versus exhaustive analysis, and Costco's limited selection traded for buying power. A usable test is whether a leader can complete the sentence about what they will not do and which capability it protects. A goal list alone is insufficient, since a real strategy must also name what will be sacrificed; otherwise it is only aspiration.
points: Strategy is defined as much by deliberate omissions as by commitments.
Each choice has an opportunity cost, so strong positions in one dimension typically mean weakness in another.
Costco is the worked example of trading variety for buying power and efficiency.
A fill-in-the-blank sentence on what will not be done, and why, serves as a credibility test.
Strategy documents should state the Why, the How and the What will be sacrificed.
quotes: Strategy is often defined less by what leaders do than by what they deliberately choose not to do. Resources such as time, money, talent, and attention are always limited.
Effective strategy always concentrates effort rather than chasing too much at once. For good leaders, every Yes contains at least one hidden No.
Costco is a case in point. The company carries far fewer products than a typical supermarket, sacrificing variety in exchange for buying power and operational efficiency.

A strategy is always more credible when a leader can easily complete this sentence: We will not do ______ because it would weaken our ability to do ______. When leaders can’t identify meaningful things they’re willing to stop, postpone, or de-emphasize, they are likely describing aspirations rather than strategy.
The goal set explains where the leader wants to go. In addition to the Why and How, a good strategy must explain What the team will sacrifice to get there.
That clarity is not a constraint on leadership. It is the very expression of it.
